# What does each parameter do?

*You'll need the fair value (chapter 3), take, clear and make (chapter 4), the skew (chapter 6), trends and the stress
test (chapter 7), the target modes (chapter 8), held-out days and the grid's `pick` (chapter 11) and the template's
`PARAMS` and `DEFAULTS` (chapter 14).*

## The story

On 15 October the template went through the stress harness, which replays each day with its prices moved,
by a trend, a shift, a spike, doubled volatility or the walls removed, and reports what the bot makes on each copy. On
Prosperity 3's round 1 it found that a trend over the day took the template from 81.3 thousand credits to 19.6
thousand going up and 14.3 thousand going down. Rainforest Resin's fixed fair of 10,000 lost 10.4 thousand each way: it
kept trading against a price that had left [(`IDEAS.md`, "Stress: what a regime change costs")]{.src}.

Two parameters came out of that run. `fixed_guard` gives up a fixed fair while the market is further than the guard
from it, and quotes around the sized mid instead. `stop_loss` flattens a product and stops it for the day once its PnL
has fallen that far below the day's high, set at about three times its worst drawdown on ordinary days, so that it
never fires on them [(`IDEAS.md`, "A fixed fair that gives way", "A loss stop per product")]{.src}.

Re-run on the template as it is now, the guard is worth what it was then. With it, the trends cost little: 66,554 and
62,214 credits against 72,674 on the days as recorded. Without it, Resin again loses 10,413 and 10,309, and the trend
days make 10,444 and 6,228. But neither parameter is free. With the guard on, a price that shifts up and stays leaves Resin 32.0 thousand with its
stop against 49.1 thousand without it: the stop fires on the move and the bot sits out a day that would have paid.
Chapter 7 tells why the stop can't help without the guard and costs with it
[(`data/stress_variants.csv`, from `arena.stress python/bots/template.py 1` with `--set`)]{.src}.

So a parameter is a bet on what the market will do, with a price on some other market. That is why each one has a
row in `IDEAS.md` saying what it was tested against, and why this chapter reads the rows before the parameters.

## The idea

### How to read an IDEAS row

The ideas file, `IDEAS.md`, is a table with four columns. **Idea** names it in bold, with where it came from. **Result on Prosperity
data** holds each test, dated, with the command that reproduces it and its numbers; a later test is added under the
earlier ones, never in their place. **Verdict here** is one of four words (the index also carries a fifth, `mixed`, that the file's header doesn't define). **Re-test on the Arena** says when and how to
try it again on the real data.

The file defines the four verdicts in its own words:

- **`kept`**: it is in the template;
- **`dropped here`**: it is not in the template, and is re-tested on the day anyway;
- **`measured`**: a fact about the data, not a strategy;
- **`open`**: tested, with no conclusion yet.

In practice "in the template" means in its settings for the products it was tested on, or available and off by
default; a dropped setting often stays in `DEFAULTS`, off, so it can be re-tested. "Dropped here" is the one to read
carefully. It is a result on one market, under its fill models, with its takers;
the file's own words are that a result there "is a prior about the Arena, not a verdict". A setting dropped on
Prosperity may be the right one on a market whose prices trend or whose takers are informed, and the re-test column
says which sign to look for. A verdict cell can name more than one word: a mode kept and one of its options dropped, or a setting dropped for one
product and kept for another. The index at the top of the file, and @fig-verdicts, take the first; the tables below
name the others.

**A kept row, read in full: "A fixed fair that gives way".** The idea is `fixed_guard`. The result has three dated entries; the story above quoted the third. On
15 October, Resin with a guard of 5: the plain days unchanged at 53,976 credits, the trend days 47.6 and 47.1 thousand
where they had been −10.4 and −10.3 thousand, the worst day +6.9 thousand instead of −3.5 thousand; but doubled
volatility and a spike up cost more than before. Later the same day, a second test found a flaw: a rival's large order
10 ticks behind the best moved the wall mid past the guard, and Resin made 15.3 thousand against 39.6 thousand without
it, so the guard now reads the sized mid, which a far order can't move. The verdict: kept, for Resin and Prosperity
2's Amethysts. The re-test: for any fixed-fair product on the day. One row holds the idea, its gain, its cost, the bug a
second test found, and when to use it.

**A dropped row, read in full: "`skew` against Kelp's long position".** Kelp sits at its limit of +50 about a tenth of
the time, and the textbook answer is to skew the quotes against the position (chapter 6). The result says three things.
On each day mirrored, prices reflected and buyers swapped for sellers, Kelp's mean position is exactly the negative of
the real day's, so the long comes from the takers' flow (34 to 36% of Kelp's trades at the touch are buys), not from
anything the bot does. The flow isn't informed: the position's correlation with the next 10 to 1,000 ticks' price
change is −0.10 to +0.18. And skew costs at every step: 18,698 credits at 0, then 18,210, 17,350 and 15,893 for 1, 2
and 3 ticks under the optimistic fill rule; 14,530 down to 9,514 under the strict one
[(`data/skew_grid.csv`)]{.src}. The verdict: dropped here, default 0, for Kelp; Pepper Root's skew of 20 is kept, with its long target (the next
section). The re-test: sweep `skew` per product, and skew
only where the same test of the position against later prices is clearly negative. It doesn't say skew is wrong; it
says that on this flow holding the position cost nothing measurable.

### The settings, group by group

The template's 71 settings fall into five groups, plus the ADAPTER's globals. Each table gives the setting's default
[(`python/bots/template.py:41`)]{.src}, what it does, and the verdict of the row that tested it, named in brackets, with
any sub-option the row drops. Two settings are left out: `reduce_only`, which flattening sets for itself, and
`day_length`, the timestamps in a day. Where a committed product overrides a default, the table gives an example, not
every override.

**Quoting: take, clear and make.**

| Setting | Default | What it does | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `take_edge` | 1 | take any book order at least this much better than the fair | kept ("The template's market maker") |
| `clear_edge` | 0; for example 5 on Picnic Basket 1 | trade back towards the target at prices up to this much worse than the fair | kept (same row) |
| `make_edge` | 2; for example Kelp 0.5, Osmium 1 | quote at least this far from the fair | kept ("Kelp `make_edge` and `take_edge`", whose own best is 1; Kelp's 0.5 was chosen later for strict fills, `docs/TODO_DONE.md`, "Tune Kelp and Squid Ink for `worse` fills?") |
| `make_inside` | 1 | quote no nearer the fair than this many ticks inside the best book quote; none: at `make_edge` whatever the book | kept as an option ("Quoting nearer fair than one tick inside the book, against rivals that do") |
| `take_edge_buy`, `_sell`, `make_edge_buy`, `_sell` | none | each side its own edge | dropped here ("Per-side edges") |
| `make_levels`, `make_step` | 1, 1 | split each side's quote over several prices | open ("Laddered quotes") |
| `take_reserve` | 0 | keep this much of the limit free for takes | dropped here ("A take reserve") |
| `join_min`, `join_ratio` | none, 2 | a quote that would join the best stands a tick back unless the queue there is deep and the other side's isn't much deeper | dropped here ("A large-tick book") |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
The quoting settings. The take edge, the clear edge and the make edge are kept: they are the market maker itself, with
Kelp's make edge at half a tick. Make inside, which stops a quote from improving on the book by more than it needs, is
kept as an option. Per-side edges, a take reserve and the large-tick gate were dropped here; laddered quotes are open.
:::

**Fair value.**

| Setting | Default | What it does | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `fair` | `sized_mid` | the method: `fixed`, `mid`, `wall_mid`, `outer_mid`, `sized_mid`, `weighted_mid` or `hysteresis_mid` | the wall, outer and sized mids kept ("Wall-mid definitions"); `weighted_mid` dropped here ("The weighted mid as fair value"); `hysteresis_mid` dropped here ("A large-tick book") |
| `wall_size` | 15 | `sized_mid`'s smallest level that counts as the market maker's quote | kept ("Wall-mid definitions": 10 to 20 within 3%) |
| `smoothing` | 0; Osmium 0.9 | an exponential average of the fair, slower nearer 1 | kept for Osmium ("A slow fair on Osmium") |
| `imbalance` | 0 | add this times the best levels' size imbalance | dropped here ("Book imbalance `ρ` and the micro-price") |
| `lin_rho3`, `lin_momentum`, `lin_window` | 0, 0, 100 | lean the fair on three levels' imbalance and on the last move | open: the settings that paid on ABIDES, a cost on Prosperity ("A `linear` fair", "A linear fair and a gate on the last move, in an agent market") |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
The fair value. The wall mid, the outer mid and the sized mid are kept, the sized mid by default, with a wall size of
15 lots. Smoothing is kept for Osmium at 0.9. The weighted mid, the hysteresis mid and the imbalance term were dropped
here. The linear terms are open: they paid in ABIDES's agent market and cost a little on Prosperity.
:::

**Inventory.**

| Setting | Default | What it does | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `skew` | 0; Pepper Root 20 | move both quotes against the position, by this much at the full limit | dropped here for Kelp ("`skew` against Kelp's long position"); Pepper Root's 20 kept with its target ("A long bias on a drifting product") |
| `size_skew` | 0 | shrink the quote that would add to the position | dropped here ("Inventory control through quote size") |
| `target` | 0; Pepper Root 80 | the position to hold; clear and skew work towards it | kept ("A long bias on a drifting product") |
| `make_size` | all the room; for example Pepper Root 10, the baskets and vouchers 0 | the largest quote | kept ("Using less than the full position limit") |
| `cross_max`, `cross_excess` | none; Hydrogel's `cross_excess` 25 | cross at most this much a tick, and clear only the part of the gap beyond it | kept ("Passive-first execution toward a target") |

The skew works on the plan's position if every order fills, its net, through one line of `make`
[(`template.py:847`)]{.src}:

::: {.eq speak="both quotes move down by the skew times the position's distance above its target as a share of the limit, rounded to whole ticks"}
$$\text{shift} = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\text{skew} \times \frac{\text{net} - \text{target}}{\text{limit}}\right)$$
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
Inventory. The size skew was dropped here, and so was the skew on Kelp: on Kelp's flow, holding the position cost
nothing a skew could save. Pepper Root keeps a skew of 20, with its long target. A target, a quote size below the limit and passive-first crossing are kept, each on the product it was
tested on: Pepper Root holds a long target of 80 with a skew of 20 and quotes of 10, and Hydrogel crosses only the part
of its bet beyond 25 lots.
:::

**Target modes.** Each sets the target in place of the static one; the first that is set wins (chapter 14).

| Setting | Default | What it does | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `level`, `level_band`, `level_exit`, `level_weight` | none, 20, none, none | hold the full limit against a move of `level_band` from a price the product returns to | kept ("Trading toward a known level"), `level_weight` dropped here; a level from the day itself open ("The day's own level where the level drifts across days") |
| `cpd_hazard` and five more `cpd_` settings | none | detect a shift of that level as it happens | dropped here ("A changepoint detector on the level") |
| `basket`, `hedge`, `hedge_ratio` | none, off, 0 | trade a basket's spread against its legs | the mode kept, taking only ("Trading a basket's spread"); hedging with the legs dropped here |
| `smile`, `underlying`, `expiry`, `smile_window` | none, none, none, 20 | price a call off a fitted volatility smile and trade its fast deviations | the mode kept ("Options: trading implied-volatility deviations from a fitted smile, delta hedging"); the smile's shape and the delta hedge dropped here |
| `follow`, `strike`, `max_cost_per_delta` | none, none, 20 | a call that holds the underlying's bet as delta | measured; the mode kept, its cost gate `max_cost_per_delta` dropped here ("What the P4 vouchers are") |
| `jump_min` and four more `jump_` settings | none | fade jumps that snap back | kept ("Fading jumps that snap back") |
| `copy`, `copy_hold`, `copy_edge` | none, none, 5 | follow named traders | kept ("Following informed counterparties") |
| `copy_sizes`, `copy_warmup` | none, 100 | follow a nameless informed trader by its trade size | measured ("A nameless informed-trade detector") |
| `gate_move`, `gate_window` | none, 20 | pull the side a recent move runs over | open ("A linear fair and a gate on the last move, in an agent market") |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
The target modes. Trading towards a known level, a basket's spread, an option's smile, jumps that snap back and named
informed traders are all kept as modes, each off until a product sets it. The changepoint detector was dropped here.
Following an option's underlying and the nameless informed-trader detector are measured; the day's own level and the
gate on the last move are open.
:::

**Protection and the close.**

| Setting | Default | What it does | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stop_loss`, `stop_edge` | none; for example Kelp 1,200, Resin 1,000, Hydrogel 48,000 | flatten and stop for the day once the day's PnL is this far below its high | kept ("A loss stop per product") |
| `fixed_fair`, `fixed_guard` | none; Resin 10,000 and 5 | a fixed fair, given up while the sized mid is further than the guard from it | kept ("A fixed fair that gives way") |
| `level_guard` | none | drop a level bet once the price is many bands away | dropped here ("Dropping a level bet once the price is far from the level") |
| `vol_guard` | none | plain market making while volatility is high | dropped here ("A volatility guard") |
| `flatten_from`, `flatten_edge` | none | from this timestamp, work the position to zero, quoting only the side that reduces it | kept, off ("Flattening before the close") |
| `flatten_keep`, `flatten_widen` | none, 0 | keep a small position at the close instead | dropped here ("Keeping a small position at the close") |
| `limit` | 50, a placeholder | the position limit, the exchange's, required in every entry | a rule, not a choice |

::: {.content-visible when-format="audio"}
Protection and the close. The loss stop and the guard on a fixed fair are kept, each set per product from the stress
test. Flattening before the close is kept but off, since Prosperity values the close at the mid. The level guard, the
volatility guard and keeping a small position at the close were dropped here. The limit is the exchange's rule, and an
entry without one is refused.
:::

**The ADAPTER's globals.** `DELAY` (0) and `ORDERS_REST` (off) switch on EXECUTION's counting of orders on their way;
the row "Orders that arrive a tick late" is open, since the Arena's timing is unknown. `MAX_RESTING` (none) is the
exchange's cap on working orders; the row "Order caps" measured that the template needs about three orders a product a
tick.

[(`data/parameters.csv`)]{.src}.

The pattern is the one the stress story ends on. What is kept is mostly the plain market maker and the modes that
each answer one kind of product; what is dropped is mostly the refinement the literature recommends for a market
unlike Prosperity's, inventory skew against uninformed flow, the micro-price, guards against regimes that never came. Those are the rows the
Arena may turn over.

### Changing one on the day

The runbook gives the order. New products go into `PARAMS` by the wiki's day-one page (T+0:30), after the diagnose
tool's suggest option has proposed an entry for each (T+0:15); a setting changes only to the grid's `pick` (T+1:00);
and each `stop_loss` is set to about three times the plain drawdown the stress tool prints (T+1:30)
[(`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round")]{.src}. The rows themselves are re-tested every round: down the index, every row whose
"Re-test on the Arena" condition fits the round's products [(`IDEAS.md`, "Keeping it up to date"; `ON_THE_DAY.md`,
"Every round", "Re-test the ideas register")]{.src}.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
`DEFAULTS` is a config's defaults, `PARAMS` the per-dataset overrides, and an `IDEAS.md` row an ablation: one switch,
the baseline beside it, the command to rerun it. "Dropped here" is an ablation that lost on one validation set, which
in ML you'd keep in the search space for the next dataset, not delete; that is the file's rule too. Where the analogy
breaks: these settings interact through the fill model, which is itself unknown (chapter 10), so an ablation's sign can
flip between two simulators of the same data, and the next dataset, the Arena, is drawn from a different
distribution by design.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}
- Every setting and its comment: `python/bots/template.py`, `DEFAULTS` (line 41) and `PARAMS` (line 161).
- A product's settings that can't matter: `arena.validate` prints them (`param_conflicts`).
- The rows by verdict: `IDEAS.md`'s index, its first 150 lines; rebuilt by `uv run python -m experiments.ideas_index`.
- This chapter's figure: `uv run python docs/guidebook/book/scripts/make_data.py --only parameters` parses the verdicts again.
- The stress test with a setting switched off: `uv run python -m arena.stress BOT DAYS --set PARAMS.<P>.fixed_guard=None`.
:::
